The '''cosmological scale factor''', often denoted by $a(t)$, describes the history of the [[cosmic expansion]] over time in the [[standard cosmology model]].

It is described by the [[1st Friedmann equation]]. 

By convention, at current [[cosmic time]],

$$
a(t_0)=1.
$$

<blockquote>
Intuitively, if at given times $t_1,t_2$, $a(t_1)=0.5,\, a(t_2)=0.25$, then the [[Universe]] was half/one-fourth of its size today.
</blockquote>

<ref>{{#cite:Q2580}}</ref>

== Cosmic expansion history ==

=== Matter-dominated expansion: $a(t) \propto t^\frac{2}{3}$ ===

In this scenario, the universe expands at a decreasing rate.
{{Hidden proof}}

According to the [[1st Friedmann equation]] (1),

{{#content:Q2574}}

For clarity, consider also its variation, the [[matter budget equation]] (2):

{{#content:Q2629}}

Hence when $\Omega_M \gg \Omega_R,\Omega_\Lambda,\Omega_K$:

$$
\left(\frac{\dot{a}}{a}\right)^2 \simeq \frac{8\pi G}{3c^2}(\rho_M)
$$

By [[cosmological fluid#Three_species|the conservation equation of cosmological fluid]],

$$
\rho_M\propto a^{-3} \\
\Rightarrow 
\left(\frac{\dot{a}}{a}\right)^2 \propto a^{-3} \\
\frac{\dot{a}}{a} \propto a^{-\frac{3}{2}}\\
\dot{a} \propto a^{-\frac{1}{2}} \\
\dot{a}dt \propto a^{-\frac{1}{2}}dt
$$

Notice $\dot a = \frac{da}{dt}$,

$$
da \propto a^{-\frac{1}{2}}dt \\
a^\frac{1}{2} da \propto dt \\
\int a\frac{1}{2} da \propto \int dt \\
a^\frac{3}{2} \propto t \\
a \propto t^\frac{2}{3}
$$

{{End hidden}}
<ref>{{#cite:Q2580}}</ref>

=== Radiation-dominated expansion: $a(t) \propto t^\frac{1}{2}$ ===

In this scenario, the universe expands at a decreasing rate, similar to in matter-dominated expansion.

{{Hidden proof}}

Proved similar to for [[cosmological scale factor#Matter-dominated_expansion:|matter-dominated expansion]].

{{End hidden}}

=== Negative-curvature-dominated expansion ($k<0$: $a(t) \propto t$) ===

In this scenario, the universe expands at a constant rate.

{{Hidden proof}}
Again consider the [[1st Friedmann equation]] and the [[matter budget equation]], similar to in proof for [[cosmological scale factor#Matter-dominated_expansion:|matter-dominated expansion]],

When $\Omega_k \gg \Omega_M, \Omega_R,\Omega_\Lambda$:

$$
\left(\frac{\dot{a}}{a}\right)^2 \simeq -\frac{kc^2}{a^2} \\
\Rightarrow \left(\frac{\dot{a}}{a}\right)^2 \propto -ka^2 \\
\Rightarrow \dot{a} \propto -k \\
\because k<0 \Rightarrow -k > 0
\Rightarrow \dot{a} \propto 1 \\
$$

Since $\dot a = \frac{da}{dt}$

$$
\frac{da}{dt} \propto 1 \\
\Rightarrow da \propto dt \\
\Rightarrow a \propto t
$$

{{End hidden}}

=== Positive-curvature-dominated expansion ($k>0$: $a(t) \propto -t$) ===

In this scenario, the universe contracts.

{{Hidden proof}}
Same process as proof for [[cosmological scale factor#Negative-curvature-dominated_expansion_(:_)|negative-curvature-dominated expansion]].

The only difference is

$$
\because k>0 \Rightarrow -k < 0
\Rightarrow \dot{a} \propto -1 \\
$$
{{End hidden}}

=== Cosmological-constant-dominated expansion ($k>0$: $a(t) \propto e^\sqrt{\frac{\Lambda t}{3}}$) ===

In this scenario, the universe expands with exponential acceleration.

{{Hidden proof}}
Again consider the [[1st Friedmann equation]] and the [[matter budget equation]], similar to in proof for [[cosmological scale factor#Matter-dominated_expansion:|matter-dominated expansion]],

When $\Omega_\Lambda \gg \Omega_M, \Omega_R,\Omega_k$:

$$
\left(\frac{\dot{a}}{a}\right)^2 \simeq \frac{\Lambda}{3} \\
\Rightarrow \left(\frac{\dot{a}}{a}\right)^2 \propto \frac{\Lambda}{3} \\
\Rightarrow \frac{\dot{a}}{a} \propto \sqrt{\frac{\Lambda}{3}} \\
$$

By definition of the [[cosmological parameter]],

$$
\Lambda \propto \rho_\Lambda
$$

Since $\dot a = \frac{da}{dt}$

$$
\frac{da}{a\,dt} \propto \sqrt{\frac{\Lambda}{3}} \\
\Rightarrow \frac{1}{a} da \propto \sqrt{\frac{\Lambda}{3}} dt \\
\Rightarrow \int \frac{1}{a} da \propto \int \sqrt{\frac{\Lambda}{3}} dt \\
$$

By [[cosmological fluid#Three_species|the conservation equation of the cosmological fluid]]

$$
\rho_\Lambda=\text{constant} \Rightarrow \Lambda=\text{constant}, \\
$$

hence

$$
\ln a \propto \sqrt{\frac{\Lambda}{3}} t\\
a \propto e^\sqrt{\frac{\Lambda}{3}} t
$$

<blockquote>
If you happen to read ''[[Source:An overview of cosmology: Summer Student Lectures 2002-2004 (Book)|An overview of cosmology: Summer Student Lectures 2002-2004]]'' (one of the sources consulted to construct this page), note their equation 2.6 contains a typographic error, wrongly omitting the square root.

PS: despite this small error, that book is a marvelous introduction to modern cosmology.
</blockquote>
{{End hidden}}
